title: Matrices and Their Operations
description: What a matrix is, how to add, scale and multiply them, and why Ax is a combination of the columns.
objectives: Read the size and entries of a matrix.
Add, subtract and scale matrices.
Multiply matrices row by column.
Read Ax as a linear combination of the columns.
Know which rules hold and that AB ≠ BA.

blocks.text: Matrices: a row of column vectors

blocks.markdown:
:::card The big idea
A **matrix** is a grid of numbers. Read it column by column and it is a **set of vectors** standing side by side. Everything we asked about vectors we can now ask about a matrix.
:::

blocks.title: Ax is a combination of the columns
blocks.source:
TRY IT: A MATRIX TIMES A VECTOR

Ax is a combination of the columns

Pick x. Walk x₁ times column 1, then x₂ times column 2.

blocks.markdown:
### In this lesson
1. Size and entries
2. Adding and scaling matrices
3. Multiplying: row by column
4. $A\mathbf{x}$ as a **linear combination** of the columns
5. Properties, and why order matters

:::card Size
A matrix with $m$ rows and $n$ columns is an $m \times n$ matrix. Rows come first.
:::

:::card Entries
$a_{ij}$ is the entry in row $i$, column $j$.

For $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$, the size is $2 \times 3$ and $a_{13} = 4$.
:::

| Name | What it looks like |
|---|---|
| Square | $n \times n$ |
| Zero matrix $O$ | every entry $0$ |
| Identity $I$ | $1$ down the diagonal, $0$ elsewhere |
| Diagonal | non-zero entries only on the diagonal |

:::card Addition
Same size only. Add entry by entry:
$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$
:::

:::card Scalar multiple
Multiply every entry:
$$3\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 12 \\ -6 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$
:::

These are the vector rules from Vector Basics, applied to every column at once.

questions.explanation:
:::card Rows first
There are **3 rows** and **2 columns**, so the size is $3 \times 2$.
:::

:::card Step 1: Scale
$$2\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -6 \\ 0 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$$
:::

:::card Step 2: Subtract entry by entry
$$\begin{bmatrix} 2 - 2 & -6 - 1 \\ 0 - 5 & 8 - 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -7 \\ -5 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$$
:::

blocks.title: Multiplying two matrices
blocks.source:
WATCH: ROW BY COLUMN

Multiplying two matrices

Press Next or Play. Each stage fills one entry.

blocks.markdown:
:::card The rule
Entry $(i, j)$ of $AB$ = row $i$ of $A$ **dot** column $j$ of $B$.
:::

:::card When it works
$A$ is $m \times n$ and $B$ is $n \times p$: the inside numbers match. The answer is $m \times p$.
:::

:::card Order matters
In general $AB \neq BA$.
:::

blocks.text: Ax: a linear combination of the columns

blocks.markdown:
:::card Look at one product
$$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = x_1\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + x_2\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
:::

:::card Why this matters
$A\mathbf{x}$ is always a **linear combination of the columns** of $A$. So questions about dependence of vectors become questions about matrices: put the vectors in as columns.
:::

:::card Example
$x = (2, 1)$:
$$A\mathbf{x} = 2(2, 1) + 1(-1, 1) = (3, 3)$$
This is the step 1 board with $x = (2, 1)$.
:::

| Property | Rule |
|---|---|
| Addition is commutative | $A + B = B + A$ |
| Multiplication is associative | $(AB)C = A(BC)$ |
| Distributive | $A(B + C) = AB + AC$ |
| Identity | $AI = IA = A$ |
| **Not** commutative | $AB \neq BA$ in general |

:::card A warning
$AB = O$ does **not** force $A = O$ or $B = O$. Matrices behave differently from numbers here.
:::

questions.explanation:
:::card Row 1
$$1 \times 4 + 2 \times 5 = 14$$
:::

:::card Row 2
$$0 \times 4 + 3 \times 5 = 15$$
:::

:::card As a combination
$4(1, 0) + 5(2, 3) = (14, 15)$: the same answer, built from the columns.
:::

questions.prompt: $A$ is $2 \times 3$ and $B$ is $3 \times 4$. What is the size of $AB$?
questions.explanation:
:::card Match the inside numbers
$(2 \times \mathbf{3})(\mathbf{3} \times 4)$: the inside numbers match, so $AB$ exists.
:::

:::card Read the outside numbers
The size is $2 \times 4$.
:::

blocks.markdown:
| Idea | What to remember |
|---|---|
| Size | $m \times n$: rows, then columns |
| Add, scale | entry by entry, same size only |
| Multiply | row of $A$ dot column of $B$ |
| $A\mathbf{x}$ | $x_1$(column 1) + $x_2$(column 2) + … |
| Order | $AB \neq BA$ in general |

**Next:** transpose, trace and special matrices.

**In this video**

1. Linear transformations and matrices (3Blue1Brown)

Watch it to see the ideas again in a different voice. Then take the final test.

questions.explanation:
:::card Row 1 by each column
$$2(1) + 1(4) = 6 \qquad 2(0) + 1(2) = 2$$
:::

:::card Row 2 by each column
$$-1(1) + 3(4) = 11 \qquad -1(0) + 3(2) = 6$$
:::

options: a linear combination of the rows of A
a linear combination of the columns of A
questions.explanation:
:::card From the definition
$$A\mathbf{x} = x_1(\text{column } 1) + x_2(\text{column } 2) + \dots$$
The entries of $\mathbf{x}$ are the scalars on the **columns**.
:::

questions.prompt: Which is true for all square matrices $A$ and $B$ of the same size?
questions.explanation:
:::card Distributive law
$A(B + C) = AB + AC$ always holds.
:::

:::card The traps
$AB$ and $BA$ are usually different, and two non-zero matrices can multiply to $O$.
:::

questions.prompt: Can a $2 \times 3$ matrix be added to a $3 \times 2$ matrix?
options: No, addition needs the same size
questions.explanation:
:::card Entry by entry
Addition pairs up entries in the same position, so both matrices must have exactly the same size.
:::

title: Transpose, Trace and Special Matrices
description: Flip a matrix across its diagonal, add its diagonal, and recognise symmetric, orthogonal and Hermitian matrices.
objectives: Find the transpose and use its rules.
Find the trace.
Recognise symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices.
Explain orthogonal matrices through perpendicular unit columns.
Recognise Hermitian, skew-Hermitian and unitary matrices.

blocks.markdown:
:::card The big idea
Some matrices have a **pattern** that makes them easier to work with. The transpose is the tool that names most of these patterns.
:::

blocks.title: The transpose
blocks.source:
WATCH: FLIP ACROSS THE DIAGONAL

The transpose

Press Next or Play.

blocks.markdown:
### In this lesson
1. The **transpose** $A^T$
2. The **trace**
3. Symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices
4. **Orthogonal** matrices
5. Hermitian, skew-Hermitian and unitary matrices

:::card Definition
Rows become columns: $(A^T)_{ij} = a_{ji}$. An $m \times n$ matrix becomes $n \times m$.
:::

| Rule | Statement |
|---|---|
| Twice | $(A^T)^T = A$ |
| Sum | $(A + B)^T = A^T + B^T$ |
| Scalar | $(kA)^T = kA^T$ |
| Product | $(AB)^T = B^T A^T$, the order **reverses** |

:::card Definition
For a square matrix, the **trace** is the sum of the diagonal entries:
$$\operatorname{tr}(A) = a_{11} + a_{22} + \dots + a_{nn}$$
:::

:::card Example
$$\operatorname{tr}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & 5 \\ 7 & 1 & 6 \end{bmatrix} = 4 + (-3) + 6 = 7$$
:::

:::card Rules
$\operatorname{tr}(A + B) = \operatorname{tr}(A) + \operatorname{tr}(B)$, $\operatorname{tr}(kA) = k\operatorname{tr}(A)$, $\operatorname{tr}(A^T) = \operatorname{tr}(A)$.

We meet the trace again with eigenvalues: it equals their sum.
:::

questions.explanation:
:::card Rows become columns
Row 1 $(2, -1, 0)$ becomes column 1, and row 2 $(3, 5, 4)$ becomes column 2. The $2 \times 3$ matrix becomes $3 \times 2$.
:::

:::card Add the diagonal only
$$5 + (-8) = -3$$
The off-diagonal entries $2$ and $9$ do not count.
:::

blocks.markdown:
| Type | Test | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Symmetric | $A^T = A$ | $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 7 \\ 7 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ |
| Skew-symmetric | $A^T = -A$ | $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 3 \\ -3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ |

:::card Two facts
- A skew-symmetric matrix has **zeros on the diagonal**, since $a_{ii} = -a_{ii}$.
- Every square matrix splits into the two:
$$A = \tfrac{1}{2}(A + A^T) + \tfrac{1}{2}(A - A^T)$$
:::

blocks.title: Columns that are perpendicular unit vectors
blocks.source:
TRY IT: AN ORTHOGONAL MATRIX

Columns that are perpendicular unit vectors

Turn the pair. They stay length 1 and at right angles.

blocks.markdown:
:::card Definition
$Q$ is **orthogonal** when
$$Q^T Q = I$$
so $Q^{-1} = Q^T$.
:::

:::card In vector words
Every column has length $1$, and every pair of columns is **perpendicular** (dot product $0$).
:::

:::card Link to dependence
Perpendicular non-zero columns are always **independent**. An orthogonal matrix never flattens anything.
:::

:::card The conjugate transpose
For complex entries, transpose **and** take conjugates: $A^* = \overline{A}^{\,T}$.
:::

| Type | Test | Real-number version |
|---|---|---|
| Hermitian | $A^* = A$ | symmetric |
| Skew-Hermitian | $A^* = -A$ | skew-symmetric |
| Unitary | $A^* A = I$ | orthogonal |

:::card Example
$$H = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 - i \\ 1 + i & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$
Transpose: the corner entries swap. Conjugate: $1 + i$ becomes $1 - i$ and back. We get $H$ again, so $H$ is **Hermitian**. The diagonal of a Hermitian matrix is always real.
:::

questions.explanation:
:::card Test Aᵀ = −A
$$\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -5 \\ 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix}^T = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = -\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -5 \\ 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$
:::

:::card The others
The first has $1$s on the diagonal, so it cannot be skew-symmetric. The third is symmetric.
:::

options: Yes: its columns are perpendicular unit vectors
No: it has zeros on the diagonal
questions.explanation:
:::card Check the columns
$(0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$ both have length $1$, and $(0, 1) \cdot (1, 0) = 0$.
:::

:::card So
$Q^T Q = I$: orthogonal. It can be symmetric too; the two are not opposites.
:::

blocks.markdown:
| Matrix | Test |
|---|---|
| Transpose $A^T$ | rows become columns; $(AB)^T = B^T A^T$ |
| Trace | sum of the diagonal |
| Symmetric / skew | $A^T = A$ / $A^T = -A$ |
| Orthogonal | $Q^T Q = I$: perpendicular unit columns |
| Hermitian / skew-Hermitian | $A^* = A$ / $A^* = -A$ |
| Unitary | $A^* A = I$ |

**Next:** determinants, the number that detects dependence.

**In this video**

1. Transpose of a matrix

Watch it to see the ideas again in a different voice. Then take the final test.

questions.explanation:
:::card The order reverses
Transposing a product reverses the order: $(AB)^T = B^T A^T$. This mirrors taking off socks and shoes: the last on comes off first.
:::

:::card From the test
$A^T = -A$ means $a_{ii} = -a_{ii}$ on the diagonal, so $a_{ii} = 0$.
:::

questions.prompt: Why are the columns of an orthogonal matrix independent?
questions.explanation:
:::card Perpendicular means new directions
Each column is at $90°$ to every other, so none can be a scalar or combination of the others. Their dot products are $0$, and each has length $1$.
:::

:::card Use the rules
$$\operatorname{tr}(2A + B) = 2\operatorname{tr}(A) + \operatorname{tr}(B) = 2(4) + (-1) = 7$$
:::

title: Determinants
description: One number that detects dependence: the determinant as an area or volume, how to work it out, and its shortcuts.
objectives: Find 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 determinants.
Explain the determinant as an area and a volume.
Use det A = 0 to decide dependence.
Use row operations and the properties to save work.

blocks.markdown:
:::card The big idea
A **determinant** is one number that tells you if the columns of a square matrix are **dependent**. It is zero exactly when they are.
:::

blocks.title: A 2 × 2 determinant measures the parallelogram
blocks.source:
TRY IT: THE DETERMINANT IS AN AREA

A 2 × 2 determinant measures the parallelogram

The columns of the matrix are a and b. Pick a pair.

blocks.markdown:
### In this lesson
1. $2 \times 2$: the determinant is an **area**
2. $3 \times 3$: expansion by cofactors
3. $\det = 0$ means **dependent** columns
4. Properties that save work

:::card The formula
$$\det\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = ad - bc$$
:::

:::card What it measures
$|\det|$ is the **area** of the parallelogram built on the two columns. You met this number before: it is the size of the cross product of the columns.
:::

:::card So
Area $0$ means the columns lie on one line: **dependent**.
:::

blocks.title: A 3 × 3 determinant, one term at a time
blocks.source:
WATCH: EXPANSION BY COFACTORS

A 3 × 3 determinant, one term at a time

Press Next or Play.

blocks.markdown:
:::card Cofactor expansion
$$\det A = a_{11}C_{11} + a_{12}C_{12} + a_{13}C_{13}$$
:::

:::card Cofactor
$C_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j} M_{ij}$, where the minor $M_{ij}$ is the determinant left after covering row $i$ and column $j$.
:::

:::card Sign pattern
$$\begin{bmatrix} + & - & + \\ - & + & - \\ + & - & + \end{bmatrix}$$
You may expand along **any** row or column.
:::

:::card The link
For a $3 \times 3$ matrix with columns $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$:
$$\det A = \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})$$
the **scalar triple product**. It is the volume of the box the columns build.
:::

| det A | Columns | Box |
|---|---|---|
| $\neq 0$ | independent | real volume |
| $= 0$ | dependent | flat |

:::card This works in any size
For a $4 \times 4$ or bigger matrix we cannot draw the box, but the rule stays: $\det A = 0$ exactly when the columns are dependent.
:::

questions.explanation:
:::card Determinant
$$6 \times 2 - 3 \times 4 = 12 - 12 = 0$$
:::

:::card Check by eye
Column 1 $(6, 4)$ is $2 \times$ column 2 $(3, 2)$: the scalar check agrees. **Dependent**.
:::

:::card Expand along row 2
Row 2 has only one non-zero entry, the $3$ in position $(2, 2)$ with sign $+$:
$$3 \times \det\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = 3 \times (1 - 8) = -21$$
:::

:::card Tip
Expand along the row or column with the **most zeros**.
:::

blocks.markdown:
| Property | Effect on det |
|---|---|
| Swap two rows | sign flips |
| Multiply one row by $k$ | det is multiplied by $k$ |
| Add a multiple of one row to another | **no change** |
| Two equal rows, or a zero row | det $= 0$ |
| Triangular matrix | product of the diagonal |
| $\det(AB)$ | $\det A \times \det B$ |
| $\det(A^T)$ | $\det A$ |

:::card Why two equal rows give zero
Two equal rows are dependent. The determinant notices dependence in **rows** as well as columns.
:::

### Find $\det\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 5 & 7 \\ 1 & 4 & 9 \end{bmatrix}$ using row operations

:::card Step 1: Clear column 1
$R_2 - 2R_1 = (0, 1, 1)$ and $R_3 - R_1 = (0, 2, 6)$. Adding multiples of rows changes nothing:
$$\det\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$$
:::

:::card Step 2: Clear column 2
$R_3 - 2R_2 = (0, 0, 4)$:
$$\det\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$$
:::

:::card Step 3: Triangular
$$\det = 1 \times 1 \times 4 = 4$$
Not zero: the columns are **independent**.
:::

questions.prompt: $\det A = 5$. What is $\det B$ if $B$ is $A$ with two rows swapped?
questions.explanation:
:::card Row swap
Swapping two rows flips the sign: $\det B = -5$.
:::

:::card Triangular
All entries below the diagonal are $0$, so multiply the diagonal:
$$2 \times 3 \times (-2) = -12$$
:::

blocks.markdown:
| Idea | What to remember |
|---|---|
| $2 \times 2$ | $ad - bc$, the area of the column parallelogram |
| $3 \times 3$ | cofactor expansion along any row or column |
| Meaning | $3 \times 3$ det = scalar triple product = volume |
| Dependence | $\det A = 0$ exactly when the columns are dependent |
| Shortcuts | row operations, triangular = product of diagonal |

**Next:** inverse matrices, which exist only when $\det A \neq 0$.

**In this video**

1. The determinant (3Blue1Brown)

Watch it to see the ideas again in a different voice. Then take the final test.

questions.explanation:
:::card Expand along row 1
$$2\det\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} - 1\det\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} + 0$$
:::

:::card Work it out
$$2(6 - 1) - 1(2 - 0) = 10 - 2 = 8$$
:::

questions.prompt: The columns of a $3 \times 3$ matrix lie in one plane. Then…
questions.explanation:
:::card Volume
The determinant is the volume of the box the columns build. Columns in one plane make a flat box: volume $0$.
:::

questions.prompt: Which row operation leaves the determinant unchanged?
options: Adding 3 times one row to another
questions.explanation:
:::card The safe operation
Adding a multiple of one row to another never changes the determinant. That is why row reduction is a fast way to find it.
:::

:::card Product rule
$$\det(AB) = \det A \times \det B = 2 \times (-3) = -6$$
:::

title: Inverse Matrices
description: Undo a matrix: the 2 × 2 formula, the cofactor method for 3 × 3, and why dependent columns mean no inverse.
objectives: Explain what an inverse does.
Find 2 × 2 inverses with the formula.
Find 3 × 3 inverses with cofactors.
Explain why det A = 0 means no inverse.
Solve Ax = b with an inverse.

blocks.markdown:
:::card The big idea
The **inverse** $A^{-1}$ undoes $A$: $A^{-1}A = AA^{-1} = I$. It exists only when $A$ does not flatten anything, that is, when its columns are **independent**.
:::

blocks.title: An inverse undoes what the matrix did
blocks.source:
WATCH: A MATRIX AND ITS UNDO

An inverse undoes what the matrix did

The grid shows where every point goes. Blue is column 1, coral is column 2.

blocks.markdown:
### In this lesson
1. What an inverse does
2. The $2 \times 2$ formula
3. When there is **no** inverse
4. The cofactor method for $3 \times 3$
5. Checking your answer

:::card The formula
$$\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}$$
Swap the diagonal, negate the other two, divide by the determinant.
:::

### Example: $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

:::card Step 1: Determinant
$$\det A = 2 \times 1 - 1 \times 1 = 1$$
:::

:::card Step 2: Swap and negate
$$A^{-1} = \frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$
This is the matrix that undid $A$ on the board.
:::

:::card Singular matrices
If $\det A = 0$, the formula divides by zero. $A$ has **no inverse**, and we call it **singular**.
:::

:::card Why, in dependence words
$\det A = 0$ means the columns are **dependent**. $A$ squashes the plane onto a line (or space onto a plane), and many points land on the same spot. Nothing can sort them back out.
:::

| $\det A$ | Columns | Inverse |
|---|---|---|
| $\neq 0$ | independent | exists |
| $= 0$ | dependent | none |

questions.explanation:
:::card Step 1: Determinant
$$3 \times 3 - 2 \times 4 = 9 - 8 = 1$$
:::

:::card Step 2: Swap and negate
$$\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ -4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$
:::

:::card Look first
Column 2 $(-6, 3)$ is $-3 \times$ column 1 $(2, -1)$: dependent.
:::

:::card Confirm
$$2 \times 3 - (-6)(-1) = 6 - 6 = 0$$
Singular, so no inverse.
:::

blocks.title: A 3 × 3 inverse, step by step
blocks.source:
WATCH: THE COFACTOR METHOD

A 3 × 3 inverse, step by step

Press Next or Play.

blocks.markdown:
:::card The method
1. Find $\det A$. If it is $0$, stop: no inverse.
2. Find all nine cofactors $C_{ij}$.
3. Transpose: $\operatorname{adj} A = C^T$.
4. Divide: $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{\det A}\operatorname{adj} A$.
5. Check that $AA^{-1} = I$.
:::

| Rule | Statement |
|---|---|
| Unique | a matrix has at most one inverse |
| Inverse of inverse | $(A^{-1})^{-1} = A$ |
| Product | $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$, the order reverses |
| Transpose | $(A^T)^{-1} = (A^{-1})^T$ |
| Determinant | $\det(A^{-1}) = \dfrac{1}{\det A}$ |

:::card Using an inverse
If $A$ is invertible, $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution:
$$\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$$
:::

questions.explanation:
:::card Rule
$$\det(A^{-1}) = \frac{1}{\det A} = \frac{1}{4}$$
because $\det(A)\det(A^{-1}) = \det(I) = 1$.
:::

:::card Step 1: Inverse
From the example, $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.
:::

:::card Step 2: Multiply
$$\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 - 3 \\ -5 + 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
:::

:::card Check
$2(2) + 1 = 5$ and $2 + 1 = 3$. ✓
:::

blocks.markdown:
| Idea | What to remember |
|---|---|
| Inverse | $AA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I$ |
| $2 \times 2$ | swap the diagonal, negate the rest, divide by $\det$ |
| $3 \times 3$ | cofactors → transpose → divide by $\det$ |
| No inverse | $\det A = 0$: dependent columns |
| Solving | $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ |

**Next:** systems of equations and row reduction, the dependence test for any size.

blocks.src: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uQhTuRlWMxw | Inverse matrices, column space and null space (3Blue1Brown)

blocks.markdown:
**In this video**

1. Inverse matrices, column space and null space (3Blue1Brown)

Watch it to see the ideas again in a different voice. Then take the final test.

questions.explanation:
:::card Step 1: Determinant
$$4 \times 2 - 2 \times 3 = 8 - 6 = 2$$
:::

:::card Step 2: Swap, negate, divide
$$\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$$
:::

questions.prompt: A matrix has no inverse exactly when…
questions.explanation:
:::card Dependence again
Dependent columns mean $\det A = 0$, and the matrix flattens space. A flattened space cannot be undone.
:::

:::card The order reverses
To undo "first $B$, then $A$", undo $A$ first, then $B$: $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$.
:::

questions.prompt: In the cofactor method, the adjugate is…
options: the transpose of the cofactor matrix
questions.explanation:
:::card Adjugate
$\operatorname{adj} A = C^T$, the **transpose** of the cofactor matrix. Then $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{\det A}\operatorname{adj} A$.
:::

title: Systems of Equations and Row Reduction
description: Solve systems with row operations, read one, none or infinitely many solutions, and test dependence in any dimension.
objectives: Write a system as Ax = b and as an augmented matrix.
Use the three row operations.
Reach row-echelon and reduced row-echelon form.
Decide between one, none and infinitely many solutions.
Test any set of vectors for dependence by row reduction.

blocks.text: Systems of equations and row reduction

blocks.markdown:
:::card The big idea
Every system of linear equations is $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$: which combination of the columns of $A$ makes $\mathbf{b}$? **Row reduction** answers it, and it is also the dependence test that works in **any** dimension.
:::

blocks.title: Row reduction, one move at a time
blocks.source:
WATCH: GAUSS-JORDAN ELIMINATION

Row reduction, one move at a time

Press Next or Play. Every board stays visible.

blocks.markdown:
### In this lesson
1. Linear equations and $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$
2. The three row operations
3. Row-echelon and reduced row-echelon form
4. One, none or infinitely many solutions
5. Row reduction as the **dependence test**

:::card A linear equation
Unknowns appear only to the first power, with no products of unknowns and none in a denominator. $3x - 2y + z = 4$ is linear; $xy = 2$ is not.
:::

:::card The matrix form
$$\begin{aligned} x + y + z &= 6 \\ 2x + y - z &= 1 \\ x + 2y + z &= 8 \end{aligned} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 1 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}$$
:::

| Operation | Example | Why it is allowed |
|---|---|---|
| Swap two rows | $R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2$ | the order of equations does not matter |
| Multiply a row by $k \neq 0$ | $R_2 \to -R_2$ | both sides of an equation scale together |
| Add a multiple of one row to another | $R_3 \to R_3 - 2R_1$ | adding true equations gives a true equation |

:::card Two target shapes
- **Row-echelon form:** a staircase of leading $1$s, with zeros **below** each.
- **Reduced row-echelon form:** zeros **above and below** each leading $1$. Getting there is **Gauss-Jordan elimination**.
:::

questions.prompt: Which matrix is in reduced row-echelon form?
questions.explanation:
:::card Check each leading 1
In the first matrix each leading $1$ has zeros above and below it.
:::

:::card The others
The second has a $3$ above the second leading $1$: row-echelon but not reduced. The third has its leading $1$s out of staircase order.
:::

:::card Multiplying by zero
$k$ must not be $0$. Multiplying a row by $0$ throws the equation away and changes the solutions.
:::

blocks.markdown:
| What the reduced matrix shows | Solutions |
|---|---|
| A leading $1$ in every column of $A$ | **exactly one** |
| A row $[0 \ 0 \ 0 \mid c]$ with $c \neq 0$ | **none**: it says $0 = c$ |
| A column of $A$ with no leading $1$ | **infinitely many**: that unknown is free |

### Example: $\left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 7 \end{array}\right]$

:::card Step 1: Reduce
$R_2 \to R_2 - 2R_1$ gives $\left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right]$
:::

:::card Step 2: Read row 2
$0x + 0y = 1$ is impossible: **no solution**. The two left-hand rows are dependent (one is twice the other), but the answers do not match.
:::

blocks.text: Row reduction: the dependence test for any size

blocks.title: Row reduction finds hidden dependence
blocks.source:
WATCH: THE TEST FOR ANY SIZE

Row reduction finds hidden dependence

Press Next or Play.

blocks.markdown:
:::card The test
1. Put the vectors in as **rows**.
2. Row reduce.
3. A **zero row** appears: **dependent**.
4. No zero row: **independent**.
:::

:::card Why it works
Row operations only build combinations of the rows. Reaching a zero row means some combination of the vectors gave $\mathbf{0}$ without all the scalars being zero.
:::

:::card Any size
This works for 4D, 5D or any number of vectors: no pictures needed.
:::

questions.explanation:
:::card Step 1: Clear column 1
$R_2 - 2R_1 = (0, 0, 1, 1)$ and $R_3 - 3R_1 = (0, 0, 1, 1)$.
:::

:::card Step 2: Clear again
$R_3 - R_2 = (0, 0, 0, 0)$: a zero row.
:::

:::card Conclusion
**Dependent**. Indeed $(3, 6, 1, 4) = (1, 2, 0, 1) + (2, 4, 1, 3)$.
:::

questions.prompt: A reduced augmented matrix has the row $[0 \ 0 \ 0 \mid 0]$ and leading 1s in only two of three columns. The system has…
questions.explanation:
:::card Read it
$0 = 0$ is always true, so nothing contradicts. One column has no leading $1$, so that unknown is **free**: infinitely many solutions.
:::

blocks.markdown:
| Idea | What to remember |
|---|---|
| System | $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$: which combination of columns makes $\mathbf{b}$? |
| Row operations | swap, scale by $k \neq 0$, add a multiple of another row |
| Echelon forms | staircase of leading $1$s; reduced = zeros above too |
| Solutions | one, none ($0 = c$), or infinitely many (free unknown) |
| Dependence test | vectors as rows, reduce, a zero row means dependent |

**Next:** Vector Algebra IV, where these tools meet vector spaces and eigenvalues.

blocks.title: Systems of Equations and Row Reduction
blocks.src: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l69YjkuUym0 | Row reduction, row-echelon form and reduced row-echelon form

blocks.markdown:
**In this video**

1. Row reduction, row-echelon form and reduced row-echelon form

Watch it to see the ideas again in a different voice. Then take the final test.

questions.explanation:
:::card Step 1: Augmented matrix
$\left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \end{array}\right]$
:::

:::card Step 2: Reduce
$R_2 \to R_2 - R_1$: $(0, -2 \mid -4)$, so $y = 2$. Then $R_1$: $x = 5 - 2 = 3$.
:::

questions.prompt: Row reduction of three vectors gives no zero row. The vectors are…
questions.explanation:
:::card The test
No zero row means no combination of the vectors gives $\mathbf{0}$ except the trivial one: **independent**.
:::

questions.prompt: Which shows a system with **no** solution?
questions.explanation:
:::card Read the row
$[0 \ 0 \mid 4]$ means $0 = 4$, which is impossible. No solution.
:::

:::card Gauss-Jordan
It continues past row-echelon form, clearing above each leading $1$ as well, to reach **reduced** row-echelon form. The solution can then be read straight off.
:::

title: Span, Basis and Coordinates
description: Everything a set of vectors can reach, the smallest set that reaches it all, and coordinates in any basis.
objectives: Describe the span of a set of vectors.
Decide whether a set is a basis.
State the dimension of a space.
Find coordinates relative to a basis.
Check a basis with a determinant.

blocks.markdown:
:::card The big idea
The **span** of some vectors is everything you can build from them. A **basis** is the smallest set that builds everything: no vector in it is wasted, because they are **independent**.
:::

blocks.title: The span of a set of vectors
blocks.source:
TRY IT: WHAT CAN YOU REACH?

The span of a set of vectors

The amber marks are every point you can build. Pick a set.

blocks.markdown:
### In this lesson
1. **Span**: everything you can reach
2. **Basis**: independent and spanning
3. **Dimension**: how many vectors a basis needs
4. **Coordinates** relative to a basis
5. Checking a basis with a determinant

:::card Definition
The **span** of $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n$ is the set of all linear combinations
$$c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\mathbf{v}_2 + \dots + c_n\mathbf{v}_n$$
:::

| Set | Span |
|---|---|
| one non-zero vector | a line through the origin |
| two independent vectors | a plane through the origin |
| three independent 3D vectors | all of 3D space |
| a dependent set | the same as the span without the extra vector |

:::card Basis (notes 2.30)
Vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n$ form a **basis** of $V$ when
1. they are **linearly independent**, and
2. they **span** $V$: every $\mathbf{w}$ in $V$ is a combination of them.
:::

:::card Dimension
Every basis of $V$ has the same number of vectors. That number is the **dimension**. 2D needs $2$, 3D needs $3$.
:::

:::card Link to the counting rule
This is why $3$ vectors in 2D are always dependent: a 2D space never needs more than $2$.
:::

questions.prompt: What is the span of $(3, -6)$ and $(-1, 2)$?
questions.explanation:
:::card Scalar check
$(3, -6) = -3(-1, 2)$: the two vectors are **dependent**.
:::

:::card So
Every combination lies on the line through $(-1, 2)$. Two dependent vectors span only a **line**.
:::

:::card Independent, but…
The two vectors are independent, but every combination has $z = 0$. They only span the $xy$-plane.
:::

:::card Dimension
3D needs **three** independent vectors.
:::

blocks.markdown:
### Example: basis $\mathbf{a} = (2, 1)$, $\mathbf{b} = (1, 3)$; write $\mathbf{w} = (4, 7)$

:::card Step 1: Set up
$$c_1(2, 1) + c_2(1, 3) = (4, 7)$$
$$2c_1 + c_2 = 4$$
$$c_1 + 3c_2 = 7$$
:::

:::card Step 2: Solve
From the first equation, $c_2 = 4 - 2c_1$. Then
$$c_1 + 3(4 - 2c_1) = 7$$
$$c_1 = 1, \quad c_2 = 2$$
:::

:::card Step 3: Read the coordinates
$$\mathbf{w} = 1\mathbf{a} + 2\mathbf{b}$$
The coordinates of $\mathbf{w}$ relative to this basis are $(1, 2)$. Relative to $\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}$ they are $(4, 7)$: the same vector, a different ruler.
:::

blocks.text: Checking a basis with a determinant

blocks.markdown:
:::card The test
$n$ vectors in $n$ dimensions form a basis exactly when they are independent, so exactly when the matrix with them as columns has $\det \neq 0$.
:::

### Example: $(1, 0, 1)$, $(0, 1, 1)$, $(1, 1, 0)$

:::card Step 1: Look first
No zero vector, no equal ratios, no common zero, no visible sum. Look further.
:::

:::card Step 2: Determinant
$$\det\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = 1(0 - 1) - 0 + 1(0 - 1) = -2$$
Not zero: the three vectors are a **basis** of 3D.
:::

questions.prompt: Basis $\mathbf{a} = (1, 1)$, $\mathbf{b} = (1, -1)$. What are the coordinates of $(5, 1)$?
Do $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 4)$ form a basis of 2D?
options: Only if we add a third vector
questions.explanation:
:::card Determinant
$$\det\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = 4 - 4 = 0$$
:::

:::card So
The vectors are dependent, $(2, 4) = 2(1, 2)$: not a basis.
:::

blocks.markdown:
| Idea | What to remember |
|---|---|
| Span | every linear combination of the set |
| Basis | independent **and** spanning |
| Dimension | the number of vectors in any basis |
| Coordinates | the scalars $c_1, c_2, \dots$ that build $\mathbf{w}$ from the basis |
| Basis test | $n$ vectors in $n$D: $\det \neq 0$ |

**Next:** eigenvectors, the special directions of a matrix.

**In this video**

1. Basis of a subspace (Khan Academy)

Watch it to see the ideas again in a different voice. Then take the final test.

questions.prompt: A basis of 3D space must have exactly…
options: any number of vectors that span 3D
questions.explanation:
:::card Dimension
3D has dimension $3$. A basis must be independent and must span, and that takes exactly $3$ vectors.
:::

questions.prompt: Adding a dependent vector to a set does what to the span?
questions.explanation:
:::card Nothing new
A dependent vector is already a combination of the others, so everything it could help reach is already reached.
:::

:::card Set up
$$c_1(1, 0) + c_2(1, 1) = (3, 2)$$
:::

:::card Solve
The second component gives $c_2 = 2$. The first gives $c_1 + 2 = 3$, so $c_1 = 1$.
:::

questions.prompt: Three 3D vectors have $\det = 0$ as columns. They…
options: span only a plane or a line
questions.explanation:
:::card Zero determinant
The vectors are dependent, so they lie in one plane (or on a line). They cannot reach all of 3D, so they are not a basis.
:::

title: Eigenvectors
description: The directions a matrix only stretches and never turns, and why Av = λv is a dependence statement.
objectives: Explain what an eigenvector and an eigenvalue are.
Read Av = λv as a dependence statement.
Interpret the size and sign of λ.
Test whether a vector is an eigenvector.

blocks.markdown:
:::card The big idea
A matrix moves vectors, and most of them **turn**. A few special directions do not turn: the matrix only **stretches** them. Those are the **eigenvectors**.
:::

blocks.title: Most vectors turn. A few only stretch.
blocks.source:
WATCH: WHICH VECTORS DO NOT TURN?

Most vectors turn. A few only stretch.

Press Apply A, then Only the eigenvectors.

blocks.markdown:
### In this lesson
1. A matrix turns most vectors
2. **Eigenvectors**: the directions that only stretch
3. $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ is a **dependence** statement
4. What the eigenvalue $\lambda$ tells you
5. Testing a candidate vector

:::card Eigenvector and eigenvalue
A non-zero vector $\mathbf{v}$ is an **eigenvector** of the square matrix $A$ when
$$A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$$
for some number $\lambda$, the **eigenvalue**.
:::

:::card Why non-zero
$A\mathbf{0} = \lambda\mathbf{0}$ for every $\lambda$, so $\mathbf{0}$ tells us nothing. It is never called an eigenvector.
:::

blocks.text: Av = λv is a dependence statement

blocks.markdown:
:::card Read it with lesson 2 in mind
$A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ says that $A\mathbf{v}$ is a **scalar multiple** of $\mathbf{v}$.
:::

:::card So
$A\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are **linearly dependent**: they lie on one line. An eigenvector is exactly a vector that the matrix sends to a dependent partner.
:::

| | $A\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ | $\mathbf{v}$ is |
|---|---|---|
| on one line | dependent | an eigenvector |
| on different lines | independent | not an eigenvector |

questions.explanation:
:::card Scalar check
$$\frac{6}{2} = 3 \qquad \frac{-3}{-1} = 3$$
:::

:::card So
$A\mathbf{v} = 3\mathbf{v}$: dependent, so $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector with $\lambda = 3$.
:::

questions.prompt: Why is the zero vector never an eigenvector?
options: $A\mathbf{0} = \lambda\mathbf{0}$ for every $\lambda$, so it says nothing
It is not in the vector space
questions.explanation:
:::card It fits every λ
$A\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0} = \lambda\mathbf{0}$ for any number $\lambda$. A definition that every matrix satisfies tells us nothing, so $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}$ is required.
:::

blocks.markdown:
| $\lambda$ | What $A$ does to the eigenvector |
|---|---|
| $\lambda > 1$ | stretches it |
| $0 < \lambda < 1$ | shrinks it |
| $\lambda = 1$ | leaves it alone |
| $\lambda < 0$ | flips it, then stretches or shrinks |
| $\lambda = 0$ | squashes it to $\mathbf{0}$: $A$ is singular |

:::card The last row
$\lambda = 0$ means $A\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ with $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}$: the columns of $A$ are dependent and $\det A = 0$.
:::

blocks.title: Is v an eigenvector? Use the scalar check
blocks.source:
WATCH: TESTING A CANDIDATE

Is v an eigenvector? Use the scalar check

Press Next or Play.

blocks.markdown:
:::card The method
1. Work out $A\mathbf{v}$.
2. Use the **scalar check** from Vector Algebra I on $A\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{v}$.
3. Same ratio $\lambda$ in every component: eigenvector.
4. A zero facing a non-zero, or different ratios: not one.
:::

questions.explanation:
:::card Test (0, 5)
$$A(0, 5) = (0, -10) = -2(0, 5)$$
Eigenvector, with $\lambda = -2$.
:::

:::card The others
$A(1, 1) = (3, -2)$ and $A(2, 1) = (6, -2)$: different ratios, so they turned.
:::

questions.prompt: An eigenvalue is $0$. What does that say about $A$?
questions.explanation:
:::card Squashed
$A\mathbf{v} = 0\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ with $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}$: a combination of the columns gives $\mathbf{0}$. The columns are dependent, so $\det A = 0$.
:::

blocks.markdown:
| Idea | What to remember |
|---|---|
| Eigenvector | non-zero $\mathbf{v}$ with $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ |
| Picture | a direction the matrix does not turn |
| Dependence | $A\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are dependent |
| $\lambda$ | the stretch factor; negative flips, $0$ squashes |
| Testing | scalar check on $A\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ |

**Next:** finding every eigenvalue and eigenvector from scratch.

**In this video**

1. Eigenvectors and eigenvalues (3Blue1Brown)

Watch it to see the ideas again in a different voice. Then take the final test.

questions.explanation:
:::card Multiply
$$A(1, -1) = (1 - 2, 2 - 1) = (-1, 1)$$
:::

:::card Scalar check
$(-1, 1) = -1(1, -1)$: eigenvector, with $\lambda = -1$. The matrix flips it.
:::

:::card Scalar multiple
One is $\lambda$ times the other, which is the definition of dependence for two vectors.
:::

questions.prompt: If $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector with $\lambda = 4$, what is $A(3\mathbf{v})$?
questions.explanation:
:::card Scaling passes through
$$A(3\mathbf{v}) = 3A\mathbf{v} = 3(4\mathbf{v}) = 12\mathbf{v}$$
So $3\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector too, with the same $\lambda = 4$. Every non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is one.
:::

questions.prompt: What does $\lambda = \tfrac{1}{2}$ do to its eigenvector?
options: Shrinks it to half its length
questions.explanation:
:::card Stretch factor
$0 < \lambda < 1$ keeps the direction and shrinks the length. Here it is halved.
:::

title: Finding Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
description: Derive det(A − λI) = 0 from first principles, then find every eigenvalue and eigenvector of 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 matrices.
objectives: Derive the characteristic equation from dependent columns.
Find eigenvalues of 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 matrices.
Find an eigenvector for each eigenvalue.
Check eigenvalues with the trace and determinant.

blocks.markdown:
:::card The big idea
We do not guess eigenvectors. One line of reasoning about **dependent columns** turns $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ into an equation we can solve.
:::

blocks.title: Why det(A − λI) = 0
blocks.source:
WATCH: FROM FIRST PRINCIPLES

Why det(A − λI) = 0

Press Next or Play.

blocks.markdown:
### In this lesson
1. **Why** $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$
2. A $2 \times 2$ example, start to finish
3. A $3 \times 3$ example
4. Two checks: the trace and the determinant

:::card Step 1: Eigenvalues
Solve the **characteristic equation**
$$\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$$
An $n \times n$ matrix gives a polynomial of degree $n$, so expect $n$ eigenvalues (counting repeats).
:::

:::card Step 2: Eigenvectors
For each $\lambda$, solve
$$(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$$
The rows of $A - \lambda I$ are dependent, so one equation always repeats. Any non-zero solution works.
:::

blocks.title: Eigenvalues first, then eigenvectors
blocks.source:
WATCH: A 2 × 2 EXAMPLE

Eigenvalues first, then eigenvectors

Press Next or Play. Every stage stays on the board.

blocks.markdown:
:::card The answers
| $\lambda$ | Eigenvector |
|---|---|
| $5$ | $(1, 1)$ |
| $2$ | $(1, -2)$ |
:::

:::card Notice
The equation for each eigenvector came from a matrix whose two rows were **multiples** of each other. That is the dependence we forced with $\det = 0$.
:::

questions.explanation:
:::card Step 1: Characteristic equation
$$(2 - \lambda)(4 - \lambda) - 3 = \lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 8 - 3 = \lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 5$$
:::

:::card Step 2: Solve
$$(\lambda - 1)(\lambda - 5) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \lambda = 1, 5$$
:::

:::card A − 5I
$$\begin{bmatrix} -3 & 3 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$$
Both rows say $x = y$.
:::

:::card So
$\mathbf{v} = (1, 1)$. Check: $A(1, 1) = (5, 5) = 5(1, 1)$.
:::

blocks.markdown:
### $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$

:::card Step 1: Characteristic equation
$A - \lambda I$ is triangular, so its determinant is the product of the diagonal:
$$(2 - \lambda)(3 - \lambda)(4 - \lambda) = 0$$
$$\lambda = 2, \ 3, \ 4$$
:::

:::card Step 2 · λ = 2
$$A - 2I = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$
Row 3 gives $z = 0$, row 1 gives $y = 0$, $x$ is free:
$$\mathbf{v} = (1, 0, 0)$$
:::

:::card Step 3 · λ = 3
$$A - 3I = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
$z = 0$ and $-x + y = 0$:
$$\mathbf{v} = (1, 1, 0)$$
:::

:::card Step 4 · λ = 4
$$A - 4I = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$
$y = z$ and $2x = y$:
$$\mathbf{v} = (1, 2, 2)$$
Check: $A(1, 2, 2) = (4, 8, 8) = 4(1, 2, 2)$.
:::

:::card The checks
- The eigenvalues **add up** to the trace: $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \dots = \operatorname{tr}(A)$
- The eigenvalues **multiply** to the determinant: $\lambda_1\lambda_2\cdots = \det A$
:::

| Example | Eigenvalues | Sum vs trace | Product vs det |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ | $5, 2$ | $7 = 4 + 3$ ✓ | $10 = 12 - 2$ ✓ |
| the $3 \times 3$ above | $2, 3, 4$ | $9 = 2 + 3 + 4$ ✓ | $24 = 2 \times 3 \times 4$ ✓ |

Use them in the exam hall to catch an arithmetic slip before you find the eigenvectors.

questions.prompt: A $2 \times 2$ matrix has trace $6$ and determinant $8$. Its eigenvalues are…
questions.explanation:
:::card Use the checks
The eigenvalues add to $6$ and multiply to $8$.
:::

:::card So
$2 + 4 = 6$ and $2 \times 4 = 8$. They are the roots of $\lambda^2 - 6\lambda + 8 = 0$.
:::

:::card Triangular
All entries above the diagonal are $0$, so $\det(A - \lambda I) = (5 - \lambda)(-1 - \lambda)(2 - \lambda)$. The eigenvalues are the diagonal entries.
:::

blocks.markdown:
| Step | What to do |
|---|---|
| Why | $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ ⇒ $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ ⇒ dependent columns ⇒ $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$ |
| Eigenvalues | solve the characteristic equation |
| Eigenvectors | solve $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ for each $\lambda$ |
| Triangular $A$ | eigenvalues are the diagonal entries |
| Checks | sum = trace, product = det |

This closes Vector Algebra: every tool, from the scalar check to the determinant, was a way of answering one question. **Can one vector be built from the others?**

blocks.title: Finding Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
blocks.src: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pZ6mMVEE89g | Example solving for the eigenvalues of a 2x2 matrix (Khan Academy)

blocks.markdown:
**In this video**

1. Example solving for the eigenvalues of a 2x2 matrix (Khan Academy)

Watch it to see the ideas again in a different voice. Then take the final test.

questions.explanation:
:::card Characteristic equation
$$(1 - \lambda)(3 - \lambda) - 8 = \lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 3 - 8 = \lambda^2 - 4\lambda - 5$$
:::

:::card Solve
$$(\lambda - 5)(\lambda + 1) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \lambda = 5, -1$$
Check: $5 + (-1) = 4 = \operatorname{tr}A$ and $5 \times (-1) = -5 = \det A$.
:::

questions.prompt: Why must $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$ at an eigenvalue?
options: $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$ with $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}$ means its columns are dependent
questions.explanation:
:::card Dependence
A non-zero $\mathbf{v}$ gives a combination of the columns of $A - \lambda I$ equal to $\mathbf{0}$. Dependent columns mean a zero determinant.
:::

:::card A + I
$$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$$
Both rows say $2x + 4y = 0$, so $x = -2y$.
:::

:::card So
$\mathbf{v} = (2, -1)$. Check: $A(2, -1) = (2 - 4, 4 - 3) = (-2, 1) = -1(2, -1)$.
:::

questions.prompt: A $3 \times 3$ matrix has eigenvalues $1$, $2$ and $5$. What is $\det A$?
questions.explanation:
:::card Product check
$$\det A = 1 \times 2 \times 5 = 10$$
:::
